Good call stopping the dishwasher immediately — that's the most important first move since it likely shares a drain line with the sink and was overloading an already-slow line.

**Do now:**
- **Don't run the sink or dishwasher again** until the drain clears or maintenance clears it. Any added water can cause the backup to overflow onto the floor or push it toward the cabinet.
- **Don't use the garbage disposal**, if there is one — running it against a clog can force water/debris up and out, or strain the motor against backed-up water.
- **Don't pour anything down the drain** — no chemical drain cleaner (Drano, etc.), no boiling water, no baking-soda/vinegar treatment. If a plumber needs to snake or disassemble the trap, chemical cleaner residue makes that dangerous (splash/fume exposure) and standing caustic liquid sitting in the pipe is a hazard to whoever opens it up.
- **Bail out the standing water** in the sink basin with a cup or small container into a bucket, just to get the level down — that's fine, it's not the same as running the tap.
- **Check under the cabinet again periodically** while you wait, even though there's nothing now — slow drains can sometimes reveal a small leak once pressure builds up in the trap.

**Good signs so far:** no sewage smell and no water under the cabinet both point toward a plain clog rather than a line break or backup from further down the stack, so this likely isn't urgent/emergency-tier, but keep the sink and dishwasher unused until maintenance looks at it either way.

Short answer: given it's load-dependent, gear-specific, and you can't verify what's happening before riding, take the bus and leave the bike for a proper look rather than riding it home.

**Why bus over ride:**
- Brakes/wheels are fine, so this isn't a stopping-power emergency — but a chain that skips under torque in specific gears can still dump your pedaling force suddenly at exactly the moments you're pushing hardest (climbs, standing starts, intersections), which is a real fall/injury risk in traffic, not just an annoyance.
- Once-per-crank skip that's load-dependent and confined to two adjacent middle cogs, showing up right after overnight rain exposure, points most likely to either (a) worn/"shark-finned" teeth on those two cogs plus a stretched chain riding up under torque, or (b) rear derailleur indexing nudged off by cable/housing swelling from moisture — both are things you could ride around by staying out of those two gears, but you won't know until you look, and you can't inspect closely right now.
- You have a no-cost, no-risk alternative (bus) — no reason to gamble on an unverified drivetrain fault when the downside is a mid-ride chain failure.

**Quick inspection once you're home (5–10 min, no special tools needed beyond maybe a ruler):**
1. Prop the bike (stand, hooks, or flip it seat/bars-down) so the rear wheel spins free.
2. Shift into each of the two problem gears and turn the crank by hand while pushing moderate resistance on the pedal with your other hand — watch where the chain sits on those two cogs specifically. Look for teeth that look hooked/pointed like little shark fins (sign of wear) versus square teeth on neighboring cogs.
3. Flex the chain at each link watching for one spot that doesn't bend smoothly (a stiff link) — this alone can cause a once-per-chain-loop skip.
4. Measure chain wear if you have a ruler: 12 full links pin-to-pin should measure 12"; if it's pulled past 12-1/16" the chain is stretched and likely the main culprit combined with those two worn cogs.
5. Sight down the rear derailleur from behind the bike to check it's hanging straight, not angled in/out (bent hanger), and give the barrel adjuster a small back-off/tighten test while pedaling in the stand to see if minor re-indexing changes the skip.
6. Note any rust film or grit on the chain/cassette from sitting out — surface rust from one rainy night alone usually isn't the cause but worth wiping down regardless.

**When you report to the shop, give them exactly this:**
- "Chain skips once per crank revolution, only under hard pedaling load, only in two of the middle rear gears — doesn't happen spinning the pedals lightly by hand."
- "Brakes aren't rubbing, both wheels are seated correctly — ruling those out."
- "First noticed after the bike sat outside overnight under a covered rack during rain."
- Ask them specifically to check: chain wear/stretch, cog tooth wear on those two specific cogs (name/count which ones if you can), rear derailleur cable tension/indexing, and derailleur hanger alignment.

That gives them enough to go straight to the likely cause instead of a generic tune-up.

Use the flat collar for a short, calm walk — don't rig a carabiner onto the cracked clasp.

**Why:** A hairline crack that already opens under hand pressure is a fatigue point; leash tension, a lunge, or a startle (Kibo runs hot on storm/heat reactivity) can propagate that crack fast, and a carabiner clipped to broken plastic doesn't add strength, it just adds a stress riser next to a weak point. A properly fitted collar with tags is a more predictable single point of failure than a compromised harness plus an improvised add-on.

**Quick checks:**

- **Collar fit** — two fingers should slip snugly under the collar; if it's loose enough to slide over his ears when backed up, tighten it before this walk. Confirm the ID tag and any license/rabies tags are actually riveted/clipped on, not just resting on the ring.
- **Hardware** — check the buckle or quick-release clasp on the collar itself for the same kind of crack/wear before you trust it; also glance at the leash clip where it attaches to the collar ring.
- **Harness replacement** — retire the cracked harness now rather than "one more wear" — don't test it on Kibo again, including at home. Order/buy a replacement sized the same as the current one; until it arrives, collar-only for short, low-key walks is the right call, especially since he's not off-leash anyway.

Keep the walk itself short and calm, consistent with how you've been handling him after stress triggers.

**15-minute moisture-gradient study**

**Setup (2 min)**
Scrap paper, quarter sheet or smaller. Pencil a 3×2 grid — 3 rows, 2 columns (same layout as before, so it's directly comparable). Label rows by moisture, narrower than last time since you're centering on what worked:
- Row 1: half-blot (one light dab, brush still slightly springy)
- Row 2: once-blotted (your baseline — one full blot on the towel)
- Row 3: double-blot (two full blots, drier than baseline)

**Lay washes (2 min)**
Same wash strength/color as before, all 6 cells at once, starting a timer the moment each cell is laid.

**Touch each edge (7 min)**
At 20 seconds per cell, touch the boundary once — no second pass, no fixing. Re-prep the brush to that row's moisture level before each touch rather than carrying over wetness from the last cell, so the rows stay distinct. Work row by row across both columns.

**Stop at the sheen cutoff (2 min)**
Let each cell sit only until the sheen dulls, per your existing cutoff — don't return after that point even if a seam looks incomplete.

**Read and note (2 min)**
Scan for which row gives the narrowest, darkest seam in *both* repeats, and flag any row that backruns or overdiffuses. That's the whole output — no filling in shapes, no additional strokes, no attempt to make the grid look finished. Treat it like a swatch card you'll set aside, not a painting in progress.

Here's how to reconcile the two records before paying anything.

## Why they don't match yet

The EOB shows the claim already **adjudicated** (processed 10/9, patient responsibility $35.00), but the portal still shows **"insurance pending"** with a balance of $95.00. That mismatch almost always means one of:

- The portal hasn't received/posted the payer's electronic response yet (lag between EOB and clinic's system).
- The clinic billed a different amount than what was allowed, and hasn't yet applied the insurance adjustment (write-off) to bring the balance down to your true responsibility.
- There's a secondary charge or separate line item bundled into the $95 that isn't part of this EOB's $145 allowed amount (e.g., a supply, brace, or a second CPT code processed separately).
- Two different service dates or claim numbers are involved and one hasn't synced.

The $95 vs $35 gap ($60) is the specific thing to chase down — don't assume the lower EOB number is automatically correct until it's confirmed against the clinic's ledger.

## Identifiers and records to pull together

Have these on hand before calling, and keep them regardless of outcome:

1. **Claim number** (from the EOB) — the primary key for the whole reconciliation.
2. **Date of service**: 10/02/2024 — confirm it's the same DOS on both documents, not a nearby visit.
3. **Billed amount** (what the clinic submitted to insurance) — the EOB should show this; the portal balance should trace back to it.
4. **Allowed amount**: $145.00
5. **Plan paid**: $110.00
6. **Patient responsibility per EOB**: $35.00
7. **Processed date**: 10/09/2024
8. **CPT/procedure codes** billed for the visit, if visible on either the EOB or an itemized statement — needed if there's more than one line item.
9. **Clinic account/invoice number** tied to the $95 portal balance.
10. **Portal claim status** and its last-updated timestamp.

Save a PDF or screenshot of both the EOB and the portal balance screen with today's date, in case either changes before this is resolved.

## Questions to ask billing (in order)

1. "Can you confirm you've received the EOB from [insurer] for claim #[X], processed 10/9/2024, showing $35.00 patient responsibility?"
2. "Does your system's current $95.00 balance already reflect the insurance payment and adjustment, or is it still showing as the pre-adjudication estimate?"
3. "Is the $95.00 for the same single visit (10/2), or does it include charges from a different date of service or a separate line item not covered by this EOB?"
4. "Once the insurance payment posts, will my balance automatically update to $35.00, or do I need to request an adjustment?"
5. "Is there a contractual write-off (the difference between billed and allowed amounts) that still needs to be applied to my account?"
6. "Can you send me an itemized statement showing the billed charge, insurance payment, adjustment, and remaining balance for this date of service?"

## What to do about payment

Don't pay the $95 now. Since the EOB explicitly states your responsibility is $35.00 and the claim has already been processed, paying the higher, stale portal balance risks overpaying and having to chase a refund. Wait for billing to confirm the payment has posted and the balance is corrected — or pay only the $35.00 once they confirm that figure matches their system, get a reference number for that payment, and keep the EOB and confirmation together in case the balance resurfaces incorrectly later.

Yes — that matches the standard diagnosis pattern. At 0.75% chain wear (past the ~0.5% threshold where cassette damage typically begins), the chain has already worn matching high spots into the cassette teeth — which is exactly the "hooking" they found on the middle sprockets, and consistent with your reported skip. Replacing only the chain at this wear level almost always causes new-chain skip/slip under load because the new chain doesn't mesh with the worn tooth profile — so replacing both together is the correct call, not upselling. Derailleur alignment being in tolerance and hanger being straight means the skip should fully resolve from the parts swap alone, no further adjustment needed.

**Pickup test before resuming your commute** (2–3 minutes in the parking lot):

1. **Full-range shift sweep, unloaded**: Pedal at an easy cadence and shift through every cog, front and rear, in both directions (low→high, high→low). Listen/feel for clean, single-click engagement — no hesitation, chain-suck, or double-shifts.
2. **Loaded pedaling in problem gears**: Stand and push hard (simulate a hill start or stoplight sprint) specifically in the middle gears where the skip was originally reported. This is the real test — a chain/cassette mismatch shows up under torque, not while spinning easily.
3. **Cross-chain extremes**: Big-big and small-small combos briefly, just to confirm no rubbing now that it's a fresh cassette (chainline can shift slightly with new parts).
4. **One hard stop-and-go**: From a near-stop, accelerate hard in a low-middle gear — this is the closest simulation to commute traffic starts and the best final check for skip.

If all of that is clean, you're good for the commute. If you get any skip or hesitation specifically under load in one or two gears, that's worth a quick trip back before you rely on it in traffic.

**Assessment: adjustment first, but treat the rotation as a real caution sign, not a shrug-off.**

The numbers you have (two-finger clearance at neck and chest, clasp holds under pressure) mean the *sizing* is right — this isn't a "too big" problem. Chest-strap rotation toward the armpit during calm indoor movement, even with correct girth sizing, is usually caused by one of two things:

1. **Under-tightened at a specific point** (often the sternum/front strap, not the girth strap) — fixable.
2. **Geometry mismatch** — the angle where the chest strap meets the girth strap doesn't match Kibo's chest shape (barrel vs. narrow chest, shoulder placement), so no amount of tightening keeps it centered — not fixable, return it.

No redness and a temporary (not persistent) fur flattening after only 10 minutes of calm movement is mild enough that you don't need to scrap the harness on this data alone. But it's also not nothing — that same migration under real walking (lunging, direction changes, pulling toward something) will have more force and more time to work with, and could progress from a flattened fur line to actual chafing, especially since Kibo runs heat-sensitive and friction + heat is a worse combination than either alone.

**Indoor test to tell the two apart, before any outdoor walk:**

1. Snug every adjustment point to the two-finger standard — not just neck and chest girth, but the sternum/front strap specifically if the harness has one. Note the exact hole/notch you land on for each strap so you can reproduce it.
2. Mark or note where the chest strap sits at rest (e.g., "centered over sternum, 1 inch below the throat").
3. Run a 10-minute mixed-movement test, not just calm standing: sit, down, stand, walk a slow figure-8, a few 90-degree turns, brief light tugging on the leash toward a toy (simulates real pulling).
4. Recheck the strap position and the fur/skin at neck, chest, and both armpits.

- **If tightening the sternum/front strap stops the rotation** and the strap stays centered through the mixed-movement test → adjustable fit, safe to proceed to a short real walk with a post-walk skin check.
- **If it still migrates toward the armpit even fully snugged**, or if you see any pinkness, warmth, or a second flattened line forming faster than before → that's the geometry mismatch signature. Return it rather than adjusting further — repeated pressure in the armpit fold is where chafing actually starts, and you won't fix an angle problem by tightening past the correct fit.

Here's a small two-wash sky study that isolates wash angle as the only variable, with the touch mechanics locked from your last exercise.

**Constants (carried over, unchanged):**
- One firm blot to the towel per edge touch (not two, not a light press)
- Touch each edge exactly once
- Touch at the 20-second mark — sheen still visible, before it dulls

**Variable: wash angle** (the tilt of the board while the sky wash is laid and setting)

**Setup**
Cut one quarter sheet into 3 cells, each ~4×6", taped on all sides so you get clean edges to judge. Board propped at:
- Cell A: flat (0°)
- Cell B: shallow tilt (~15°)
- Cell C: steep tilt (~30°)

**Per cell, same sequence:**
1. Wash 1 — pale graded sky wash (thin blue-grey), laid horizon-to-zenith in 2–3 strokes, at that cell's tilt.
2. At 20 seconds, one firm blot to the lower edge where pigment is pooling toward the tape line.
3. Let it sit until touch-dry to the back of the hand (don't force it).
4. Wash 2 — a single soft cloud shape or deepened band, dropped in wet-into-damp near the upper third, same tilt held.
5. At 20 seconds from *that* wash's edge forming, one firm blot to whichever edge is showing the most bead.

**What to watch across the three:**
- Where the pigment pools (top vs. bottom of cell) and whether the 20-second/one-blot control still catches it at that pooling point
- Whether steeper tilt moves the bead location enough that your blot is landing in the wrong place
- Any bloom — if it shows up only at one angle, that tells you the timing window shifts with tilt, not just with the wash itself

That last point is the real question this study is answering: whether "20 seconds" is a fixed number or actually a function of how fast gravity is pulling pigment to the edge.

## What it does NOT establish

- **Her real out-of-pocket total.** Premium + deductible is only the entry cost. Actual annual spend depends on copay/coinsurance tiers for her *specific* drugs, which aren't in this notice at all.
- **Whether her drugs are still covered, and at what tier.** A formulary can shuffle a drug to a higher (or lower) tier even when premium/deductible look stable — that alone can swing her costs more than the numbers shown.
- **Whether her current pharmacy is still "preferred."** "Participating" and "preferred" are different tiers in most plans — using a non-preferred pharmacy can mean higher copays even for the same drug.
- **Prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limits** on her drugs — these can change year to year and aren't disclosed in a rate notice.
- **Where she'd land relative to the coverage gap / catastrophic threshold**, which depends on her 2024 utilization plus 2025 dollar thresholds — not calculable from this letter.

## Checklist before she compares or picks a plan

**Documents to get (from the plan, not just this notice):**
1. **Annual Notice of Change (ANOC)** for 2025 — the formal year-over-year comparison document; this notice may be an excerpt of it, so confirm she has the full version.
2. **2025 Evidence of Coverage (EOC)** — full cost-sharing structure by drug tier.
3. **2025 Formulary/Drug List** — to check every drug she currently takes.
4. **2025 Pharmacy Directory** — to confirm her usual pharmacy's status (preferred vs. standard vs. out).
5. **2024 claims/EOB history or a drug spend summary** — needed to estimate what the 2025 numbers actually mean for her.

**Questions to answer for each of her current medications:**
- Is it still on the 2025 formulary? If so, what tier?
- What's the copay or coinsurance at that tier, at her preferred pharmacy?
- Any new prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limit?

**Questions about the pharmacy:**
- Is her current pharmacy preferred, standard, or dropped from network in 2025?
- If it moved tiers, what's the cost difference for her specific drugs there vs. a preferred location?

**Before she selects a plan:**
- Ask the plan (or 1-800-MEDICARE / SHIP counselor, if this is Medicare Part D) for a personalized total-cost estimate based on her actual drug list — not the generic notice.
- If comparing plans, run the same drug list through Medicare's Plan Finder (or equivalent) for an apples-to-apples 2025 estimate across options, not just this one plan's renewal terms.

A quick anatomy note first: the two-finger clearance at the neck/chest and the belly-strap gap are two different kinds of "adjustment."

**Why buckle adjustment probably can't fix the belly-strap clearance**
- Neck/chest strap fit is a *tightness* adjustment — sliding a buckle changes how snug the loop is, and that's what you correctly checked with the two-finger test.
- Belly-strap clearance from the front legs is a *position* issue — it depends on where that strap is anchored to the harness frame, which is fixed relative to the chest plate. Loosening the belly strap doesn't move the anchor point backward; it just adds slack in the same spot. That reintroduces the exact failure mode you saw on the previous harness (strap migrating toward the armpit under movement), so loosening it to "buy" clearance would trade one problem for the other.
- If this Y-front model has a separate torso-length adjustment (distinct from girth) at the chest plate, that's the only mechanism that could genuinely shift the belly strap back — worth a 30-second check of the hardware before ruling it out. If it's girth-only, the one-finger-width placement is baked into this size for a 25.5" chest, not something you can adjust away.

**Indoor test that separates "adjustable" from "wrong shape"**
Calm walking under-tests this — the strap only reveals a placement problem under full leg extension and repeated motion. Do this indoors, on leash, over 10–15 minutes:

1. 5–10 sit-to-stand / down-to-stand transitions — recheck strap position and fur after.
2. A few tight figure-8 turns and a short trot down a hallway.
3. A couple of reaches — paws up on a low step or stretching for a treat — to get full front-leg extension, which is the moment a too-forward strap is most likely to pinch or ride up.
4. After that mixed activity, run a hand along the belly-strap contact line: look for it having migrated toward the armpit (same pattern as before), any new flattening or rub line in the fur, or a shortened/choppy stride compared to his normal gait.

**Verdict rule:** if the strap holds its position and there's still no redness/abrasion after that dynamic sequence, it's a usable fit despite the tighter-than-spec clearance. If you see it start creeping toward the armpit or affecting stride, that's the same shape problem as the last harness, just less advanced — return it before an outdoor walk exposes it under more force.

**35° bead-frequency study** — same paper batch, pigment/dilution, and single sitting as before; brush condition (one firm blot), 20s edge-touch, and one-touch rule held fixed throughout. Board fixed at 35°.

Four strips, same wash, order randomized if paper allows:

1. **No wick** — let the bead sit untouched for the full wash (replicates the bloom you got).
2. **Single wick** — one blot of the lower bead at the wash's midpoint only.
3. **Fixed-interval wick** — blot the bead every ~20–30s as it reforms (matches your edge-timing window, so bead removal and edge-touch stay on the same clock).
4. **Continuous wick** — blot the bead the moment it's visibly re-forming, essentially keeping it thin throughout.

For each strip, log: number of wicks actually taken, whether a bloom/cauliflower edge appeared, and how fast the bead reformed after each wick (rough seconds). That reform-speed note is what will tell you whether "frequency" or "bead volume at removal" is the real lever.

Here's a safe sequence to get to ≥27 GB free without risking active Helio files or crossing company-data boundaries:

**1. Verify the Oct 19 backup before touching anything**
- Confirm the backup app's log shows the Desktop and Downloads folders were included (not just Documents).
- Since it's been 7 days, kick off a fresh incremental backup now (or at minimum, manually back up the Desktop Helio export folder) so anything created since Oct 19 isn't at risk once you start deleting/moving files.

**2. Clear video-call cache (6 GB) — safe, no backup needed**
- App-regenerable cache (Zoom/Teams/etc. local recordings-cache, not saved recordings). Clear via the app's own cache-clear setting or its cache folder in AppData/Library. This alone gets you to ~25 GB free.

**3. Triage Downloads (4 GB)**
- Delete installers, duplicates, and temp files (.dmg/.exe/.zip you already installed from).
- Anything unclear or work-related that isn't a duplicate: don't delete — move to your company-sanctioned storage (SharePoint/Drive workspace, network share), not a personal account.

**4. Triage Desktop exports (9 GB) — separate active from stale**
- Sort by modified date; anything actively being used for an in-flight Helio analysis stays local.
- Completed/superseded exports (old CSV pulls, prior chart iterations) get moved — not deleted — to your team's company storage (e.g., the Growth folder), since they're reproducible from source data if ever needed and this frees space without deleting anything.
- Do **not** move any of this to a personal cloud/email/drive — company-data boundary applies to raw exports even if anonymized-looking.

**5. Recheck free space**
- After cache clear (6 GB) + Downloads cleanup (partial) + moving stale Desktop exports off-disk, you should clear 27 GB. Confirm in Storage settings before starting the OS update.

**6. Only if still short:** empty Trash/Recycle Bin (moved files don't free space until emptied) and check for local Time Machine/OS snapshot leftovers, which can silently hold several GB.

This order keeps active Helio analyses untouched, keeps company data out of personal accounts, and doesn't rely on deletion until the backup is confirmed current.

- Attempting to escape the room, destructive self-injury (scratching at door/walls to the point of bleeding), or hiding in a way that seems frozen rather than settled

Here's a safe flushing sequence for after the valve work, plus what to hold off on and red flags to watch for.

**Flush in this order (cold water only first):**
1. **Start with the fixture farthest from the main shutoff** (often an outdoor spigot or a bathroom sink upstairs) — this pushes trapped air and loosened sediment out efficiently.
2. **Run each cold tap in the unit for 3-5 minutes**, one at a time, kitchen last since that's your drinking source. Cloudiness that's actually trapped air (fine bubbles that clear from the bottom of a glass up) should visibly settle within a few minutes; sediment cloudiness looks gritty/brownish and won't clear the same way.
3. **Flush each toilet 2-3 times** — this clears the fill valve and line without wasting water you'd otherwise drink.
4. **Only after cold runs fully clear for a few consecutive minutes**, move to hot water: run hot taps briefly to clear the line up to the water heater, but don't rely on this water for drinking yet — hot lines can carry heater-tank sediment stirred up by the pressure change.

**Hold off on, until cold water runs consistently clear:**
- Drinking/cooking with tap water — keep using your stored water for you, Sam, and Kibo.
- Fridge/ice-maker water and ice — same air/sediment risk, and it's easy to forget this one.
- Dishwasher and washing machine — their inlet filters can trap sediment; run them empty once water's confirmed clear if you want to flush those lines too, rather than running a load into a fouled filter.
- Kibo's water bowl — keep refilling from stored water for now rather than a freshly-run tap, since the flushing sequence.

**Call maintenance / avoid the water if you see:**
- Discoloration (brown, yellow, or black tint) that persists past ~15-20 minutes of flushing multiple fixtures, not just one.
- Sputtering/air that hasn't resolved after flushing several fixtures for a few minutes each — could mean a bigger air pocket or a partially open valve.
- Pressure that stays noticeably low rather than returning to normal.
- Any odor — rotten-egg, chemical, or strong chlorine smell is a reason to stop and call, even without a boil-water notice.
- Visible particulate/grit that keeps recurring after multiple flush cycles.

Given no boil-water notice and the pattern you're describing (cloudy → clearing, fine bubbles, normal pressure, no odor/sediment), this reads as typical post-shutoff air rather than a contamination concern — but let it run fully clear across several fixtures before trusting it for drinking. Since the guest-bath toilet has had fill-valve issues before, worth a quick check there specifically once you flush it, just to confirm it's refilling and shutting off normally post-valve-work.

**Don't ride it, even locally.** A sidewall cut that's long enough to expose casing and that visibly opens under squeeze pressure is a structural failure point, not a tread puncture — sidewalls have much thinner rubber over the casing than the tread does, and casing threads can let go suddenly under load (standing on a pedal, hitting a bump, cornering), not gradually like a slow leak. Tube pressure holding fine right now doesn't tell you anything about the sidewall's ability to survive load-bearing use. This is the same category of issue as the 8mm rear-sidewall cut you had shop-inspected instead of rode back in August.

**Deflating & transporting sequence:**
1. **Photograph first, while still inflated** — deflating will close the gap and hide exactly what the shop needs to see.
2. Remove valve cap; depress the valve core (Schrader: push pin; Presta: unscrew the tip first, then push) until air stops hissing, then press down on the tire with your palm to push out remaining air pocket by pocket.
3. Once fully flat, spin the wheel to check nothing is bulging through the cut with the tube slack — if the tube pokes through even slightly, don't reinflate at all, even a little, for transport.
4. If it's quick-release, you can pull the wheel and lay the bike/wheel flat in a car trunk or rideshare's trunk — ask the driver first if it's a sedan. For transit, check the agency's bike policy (some require the wheel removed and bagged, others just want it walked, not ridden, through stations).

**Photos/details for the shop:**
- Straight-on close-up of the cut with the tire still inflated, and a coin or ruler next to it for scale.
- A second shot squeezing the tire to show the gap opening and any casing/tube bulge.
- A wide shot of the sidewall showing tire brand/model and size markings (usually printed near the valve).
- Note for them in writing: rear tire, ~8mm sidewall cut, casing visible, gap opens under squeeze, tube currently holding pressure, tire mileage/age if you know it, and whether it's tube-type or tubeless.

**Cleaning**

- Limping or non-weight-bearing that appears or persists (rather than the paw simply being licked)
- Swelling, spreading redness, or heat around the site
- Discharge, odor, or the area looking worse instead of better over 24–48 hours
- Any sign a piece of gravel is still embedded (visible dark speck, a hard spot under the skin, or him flinching at a specific point when you press gently)
- Fever, lethargy, or appetite loss

## Cautious synthesis

- **Guidance gaps (1, 5)** cluster around the moment right after a connector action succeeds — the product confirms the mechanical step worked but doesn't tell the user what comes next or whether configuration (e.g., lifecycle-stage mapping) is correct. This is a UX/communication issue, not a data or authority issue.
- **Product-state signaling gaps (2, 3)** are about the system not clearly reflecting "done-ness" back to the user. #3 is sharper than #2: an invite action apparently isn't being credited by the checklist, which is worth a quick instrumentation check (comparable to the kind of lag/logic gap seen in [[project_helio_start_report_refresh_lag_may7]] and the open [[project_helio_start_suppression_rule_gap]]) before assuming it's just a communication problem rather than a bug.
- **Authority gate (4)** sits outside Helio's product surface entirely — this is the customer's own security review, not something a UI or checklist fix resolves. The only lever here is expectation-setting copy (e.g., acknowledging "pending your org's approval" as a known state), similar in spirit to the access-review framing already used in the HS confirmation email.

**Caveats — please treat these carefully:**
- This is qualitative coding of five open-text comments, not a quantified sample. It says nothing about how common each theme is across the applicant/signup base, and shouldn't be cited as "X% of users hit this."
- I haven't touched [[project_activation_definition]] (v3 stays integration + in-product event within 14 days) — these comments are about setup/checklist UX, not the activation metric itself, and nothing here implies the definition should change.
- Comment #3 in particular reads like it could be either a copy/communication gap or an actual state-sync bug — worth a quick log pull to distinguish before deciding which team owns a fix, rather than assuming either explanation from the comment alone.

**Activation rates (Q3, activation-v3, by onboarding path):**

| Path | Activated / Eligible | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| Guided | 54 / 72 | 75.0% |
| Partner-assisted | 24 / 30 | 80.0% |
| Self-serve | 91 / 150 | 60.7% |

**Interpretation:**

Guided and partner-assisted show higher observed activation than self-serve, but this is a descriptive cut of an unrandomized, self-selected split — not a comparison you can attribute to onboarding path quality. The group sizes are also very uneven (72 and 30 vs. 150), so the guided/partner-assisted rates rest on much thinner samples and are more sensitive to a handful of workspaces either way.

More importantly, path assignment is almost certainly confounded with workspace characteristics that independently affect activation likelihood — e.g., guided and partner-assisted onboarding tend to be steered toward larger accounts, accounts with CS/partner relationships, or workspaces with more hands-on support, any of which could drive activation regardless of the onboarding mechanism itself. Self-serve skews toward whoever signs up unassisted, which is a different population, not just a different experience.

Bottom line: this is a real, current gap in observed activation across paths, but it should be reported as "activation varies by path in this cohort" — not as "guided/partner-assisted onboarding causes higher activation" or as grounds to shift onboarding investment. Establishing a causal effect of path would need either randomized assignment or a stratified/matched comparison controlling for the segment differences likely driving path assignment in the first place.

I'd push back gently on reading the echo as settling it. Mara's lesson only ever taught the *hiding place* — "where anyone who knew me would look." It says nothing about a gate, let alone a locked one. So when the narrator closes with "I locked the gate. The key went back beneath the flat stone," we're watching two different gestures collide: the inherited, intimate one (the spot itself, unchanged since Mara) and a new one the narrator adds on top of it (the act of locking). The repetition of the hiding place doesn't cancel the lock — it sits right next to it.

That's what keeps the ending ambiguous rather than resolving it. If the narrator only locked the gate, that's a clean boundary — access denied. If the narrator only returned the key to the old spot, that's a clean invitation — access as always. Doing both means the narrator is requiring exactly what Mara's phrase already implied: not just anyone gets in, only "anyone who knew" — knew the place, knew the ritual, knew *her*. The lock filters out the general public; the key placement still leaves the door open to the specific, known person. So the ending isn't inviting *or* excluding — it's narrowing who the invitation is for, without telling us whether anyone who fits that description still exists, or is even wanted.

I'd want to ask the group: is the lock protecting the narrator from strangers, or is it protecting the ritual itself — making sure that if someone does come, it can only be someone who was actually taught to look?

# Reach-In Failure — Conservative Holding, Segregation, Logging, Escalation Plan

**Governing constraint:** the two air readings (38°F @10:30, 46°F @11:15) tell you the *unit* was drifting during that window — they don't tell you when the *food* crossed 41°F, how long it stayed there, or whether it was already elevated before 10:30. Air and food temperature lag differently (raw chicken especially), and the drift could have been linear or a step-change (door left open, compressor fault, etc.). This is a very low-risk exposure — no need for emergency vet or poison-control contact right now.

**Why the risk is low:** Onion/garlic toxicity in dogs is dose-dependent, causing oxidative damage to red blood cells. The rough toxic threshold is on the order of 15–30g/kg of onion (garlic is roughly 5x more potent by weight). For a 42 lb (~19 kg) dog, that threshold is far above what's in a single lick of gravy — you're talking about cooked, diluted seasoning amounts, not raw bulb onion. A teaspoon or less of gravy is well below any dose associated with clinical toxicosis.

**What makes this reassuring:**
- Amount is trace (<1 tsp), not raw onion/garlic in concentrated form
- He's already acting normal with none of the acute red flags (vomiting, drooling, weakness, pale gums, breathing changes, abdominal pain)

**Delayed signs to monitor anyway (out of caution, not because this dose is expected to cause them):**
Onion/garlic-induced hemolytic anemia has a *delayed* onset — signs typically don't show up until **1–5 days post-ingestion**, sometimes peaking around day 3–5. Watch for:
- Lethargy or reduced energy/appetite
- Pale, white, or yellow-tinged (icteric) gums
- Reddish-brown or dark urine (hemoglobinuria) — this is often the earliest tell
- Rapid breathing or elevated heart rate
- Vomiting or diarrhea

**Bottom line:** Given the tiny amount and his current normal behavior, no action is needed tonight. Just do a quick gum/urine color check once or twice a day through the weekend (roughly through Sunday, given today's Wednesday 11/27 timing) as routine due diligence. If any of the above signs appear, that's when to call your vet or ASPCA Animal Poison Control — not before.

Given the 3-hour gap and that both the counter (food-safety) and the 200°F roaster (drying) are problems, the cleanest fix is the "insulated cooler" hot-hold trick — it keeps the turkey safely above the 140°F danger-zone floor without any added heat or moisture loss, and it frees the roaster and oven completely for everything else.

**Hold (11:05am–~1:15pm):**
1. Let the turkey rest tented loosely for 20–30 min as normal — fine at room temp for that short window.
2. Wrap it tightly in two layers of heavy-duty foil (pour a little of the pan drippings or broth over it first if you have any, to add surface moisture before sealing).
3. Line an empty cooler with towels, nestle the wrapped turkey in, pack more towels tightly around/on top, and close the lid.

This will hold well above 140°F for 3+ hours with no active cooking, so it won't dry out or overcook — it's essentially coasting on its own retained heat, and a tightly packed cooler is a very effective insulator. This sidesteps both problems: no room-temp danger-zone exposure, no 200°F roaster slowly cooking the moisture out.

**Reheat/serve (~1:15–2:00pm):**
- Uncover, baste with pan juices or broth, and give it a short blast — either a brief stint in the roaster at its 200°F setting (tented, with a little broth in the bottom for steam) for 20–30 min just to bring the surface back up to serving temp, or a quick pass in the oven once the macaroni/stuffing/rolls come out.
- You're not "cooking" it again, just warming the exterior back up — internal temp is already well past safe minimums, so this is about serving temperature, not safety.

This avoids both failure modes you flagged: no near-3-hour room-temperature sit, and no multi-hour bake in a 200°F roaster that would toughen the meat.

Scaling factor: 14 ÷ 8 = **1.75×**

**Scaled ingredients**
- Cornmeal: 1½ cups → **2⅝ cups**
- All-purpose flour: ½ cup → **⅞ cup**
- Sugar: 2 tbsp → **3½ tbsp**
- Baking powder: 2 tsp → **3½ tsp**
- Salt: ¾ tsp → **1¼ tsp** (technically 1.3 tsp — round to 1¼, cornbread won't notice)
- Buttermilk: 1¼ cups → **2 cups + 3 tbsp**
- Eggs: 2 large → **3.5 eggs** (see below)
- Melted butter: 4 tbsp → **7 tbsp**

**The egg problem**
3.5 eggs isn't roundable without a real tradeoff — I'm not going to silently call it "4 eggs" and hide that.
- **Precise option:** use 3 whole eggs, then beat a 4th egg separately and add only half (~1.5 tbsp of the beaten egg) to the batter. Gets you the actual 1.75× ratio.
- **Simple option:** just use 4 whole eggs. The batter will be slightly richer and a touch more cake-like than the original's crumb, but for a cornbread this forgiving, most people won't notice at a family lunch.

Given it's a casual family meal, I'd go with 4 whole eggs unless you want it as close to Mom's original texture as possible.

**Pan size**
An 8-inch square pan is 64 sq in. At 1.75×, you need ~112 sq in of pan area.
- A standard **9×13 pan (117 sq in)** is the closest practical match — batter depth will be very close to the original, just very slightly shallower.
- Two 8-inch pans (128 sq in total) is a worse fit — batter would be noticeably shallower and dry out faster.
- **Recommendation: one 9×13 pan.**

**Bake time**
Don't just reuse 22–25 minutes. Because the 9×13 gives a marginally shallower batter layer than the original 8-inch pan, it may bake slightly faster.
- **Start checking at 18–20 minutes** with a toothpick in the center; pull it when it comes out clean and edges are just pulling from the pan sides. Could still land in the original 22–25 min range — just don't assume it without checking.

## Recommended custom opening: 8¼ × 11 inches

**Assumption:** I'm treating the 8.5 × 11.25″ image as roughly centered on the 9 × 12″ sheet — margins of 0.25″ left/right and 0.375″ top/bottom, with the signature sitting 0.2″ in from both the right and bottom painted edges (i.e., 0.45″ from the paper's right edge, 0.575″ from its bottom edge). Worth confirming with the shop before cutting if your margins aren't symmetric.

**Why the standard 8 × 10.5″ opening fails:** it crops 0.25″ off each side of the width and 0.375″ off each side of the height — the height crop alone (0.375″) exceeds the signature's 0.2″ inset, so it would clip the signature outright.

**The fix — don't center the window on the paper, center it on the image**, biasing the extra margin toward the top-left (where there's no signature) instead of splitting evenly:

| Side | Mat border (paper overlap) | Image crop |
|---|---|---|
| Right | 5/16″ (0.3125″) | 1/16″ (0.0625″) |
| Bottom | 7/16″ (0.4375″) | 1/16″ (0.0625″) |
| Left | 7/16″ (0.4375″) | 3/16″ (0.1875″) |
| Top | 9/16″ (0.5625″) | 3/16″ (0.1875″) |

**Result:**
- **Image crop:** only 1/16″ trimmed off the right and bottom of the painted area (blank margin, not content); 3/16″ trimmed off the left and top, also blank margin. No part of the actual composition near the signature is touched.
- **Paper overlap:** every side is ≥5/16″, well above the ~1/4″ minimum framers typically want to securely cover the sheet's edge — the left/top sides are especially generous (7/16″–9/16″).
- **Signature clearance:** the 1/16″ crop taken from the right and bottom reduces the signature's 0.2″ margin to about 0.14″ (~9/64″) of visible clearance from the mat's inner edge on both sides — comfortably positive, not flush with the cut line.

If you want more breathing room around the signature specifically, you can shift the whole opening slightly further left/up (increasing top/left borders further) without changing the 8¼ × 11″ opening size — that only adds paper overlap on the non-signature sides, it doesn't touch the signature clearance number above.

Good instinct to stop using it. Here's how to read the evidence and what to do next.

## What the evidence suggests

A GFCI tripping **specifically** with the dryer — while a lamp on the same outlet works fine — points toward the **dryer itself**, not the outlet wiring. GFCIs trip on ground-fault leakage current, and that leakage has to originate somewhere. Since the lamp draws power without issue, the outlet is successfully carrying current and detecting faults correctly (i.e., it's working as designed). Two trips on two separate attempts (not one fluke) means this is a repeatable fault, not a random nuisance trip — most likely from:
- Worn/nicked cord insulation
- Bathroom humidity/steam getting into the dryer's motor or heating element housing
- An internal short from age/wear

None of that requires visible damage to produce a real (if small) leakage current — GFCIs are sensitive enough to catch faults well before you'd see heat or scorching.

## Isolation sequence

1. **Unplug the dryer entirely** — don't leave it plugged in idle; there's no reason to keep it connected to power.
2. **Visually inspect it unpowered** — cord for nicks/fraying, plug prongs for corrosion, housing vents for anything unusual. Don't power it on to test.
3. **Confirm the outlet independently** — you already have this: the lamp ran normally after each reset. If you want more confidence, plug a second, different appliance (not the dryer) into that outlet under normal use.
4. **Don't "test" the dryer in a different outlet.** That doesn't isolate anything new — it just risks tripping another circuit or continuing to run a faulty appliance. Treat this as an appliance problem, not a "find an outlet where it works" problem.
5. **Tag/set aside the dryer as out of service** so it doesn't get used by mistake before you replace it.

## Verdict: appliance retirement, not outlet report as urgent

- **Retire the dryer.** The pattern (fault only with the dryer, GFCI functioning correctly, no fault with a control appliance) points to an internal leakage fault in the dryer. Hair dryers aren't practical to repair — replace it.
- **Outlet is not implicated as faulty**, but it's still worth a low-priority note to maintenance for their records: "GFCI in bathroom tripped twice with hair dryer on [date], confirmed outlet otherwise functions normally with a lamp." This isn't urgent — it's just good practice so there's a record if any other issue ever surfaces at that outlet, and so they can inspect the GFCI mechanism itself if they want to be thorough.
- No need for an emergency maintenance ticket given the absence of any urgent signs (see below).

## Signs that would make this urgent (any of these → unplug immediately, don't reset again, contact maintenance/an electrician right away)

- Burning smell, smoke, or scorch/discoloration on the outlet or plug
- Outlet or plug warm/hot to the touch
- Buzzing, crackling, sparking sounds
- Visible moisture inside or around the outlet
- GFCI trips instantly with no load, or won't reset at all
- Other outlets or the whole circuit start tripping too
- Any tingling sensation touching the appliance, cord, or outlet

You have none of these, which is consistent with "faulty appliance caught correctly by a working safety device" rather than a wiring hazard.

Good call blocking the link. This has all the hallmarks of an SMS phishing ("smishing") scam targeting travelers:

**Phishing indicators**
- **No checked bag exists** — the premise itself is fabricated, so there's nothing legitimate to "release."
- **Trivial dollar amount ($2.14)** — designed to feel too small to question, which lowers guard.
- **Artificial urgency** ("within 30 minutes... or return") — pressure tactic to prevent verification.
- **Sender is a random 10-digit number**, not a short code or the airline's verified sender ID that official alerts use.
- **Suspicious domain** (`airline-baghelp.co`) — not the airline's actual domain; odd TLD, generic "help" wording.
- **No corroborating alert in the airline's own app** — real baggage/payment holds show up there, not exclusively via SMS link.
- **Payment demand via link, not in-app** — airlines don't collect ad hoc fees through unsolicited text links.

**Safe verification steps (don't touch the link or reply to the sender)**
1. Open the airline's official app (or type the airline's known URL directly into a browser — don't tap anything from the text) and check for any bag alerts, holds, or payment requests. If nothing appears there, the text is fake.
2. If Mom wants a human to confirm, have her call the number printed on her actual ticket/boarding pass or the airline's official customer service line (not any number in the text) and ask if there's any bag issue on her reservation.
3. If she's still at the gate/counter, she can also just ask airline staff in person — fastest confirmation.

**Deletion**
4. Once confirmed nothing is pending, delete the text without clicking the link. On iPhone: report as junk first (see below) before deleting; on Android, just delete/block.

**Reporting**
5. Forward the text to **7726 (SPAM)** — this reports it to her mobile carrier for phishing/spam analysis regardless of carrier.
6. Report the phishing domain to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov and to the airline itself via their official "report phishing/scam" page or the number on the ticket — airlines track these to warn other customers.
7. Block the sending number on her phone.

She's safe as long as she doesn't tap the link or enter payment info — no further action needed beyond the steps above.

Here's a backward-planned schedule for one oven, three different temperatures, ending with everyone sitting down at 1:30pm.

**Key move:** since the chicken's resting time doesn't require the oven, that ~45–50 minutes becomes your window to cook the mac and cheese and rolls sequentially. That's what makes a single oven work here.

| Time | Action |
|---|---|
| **11:05am** | Chicken into oven at 375°F (90 min) |
| **12:35pm** | Chicken out. Tent loosely with foil, let it rest on a cutting board/counter. |
| **12:40pm** | Mac and cheese (covered) into oven at 350°F for 30 min — 5 min gap lets the oven cool from 375°F. |
| **12:45pm** | Marcus arrives — no conflict, mac and cheese is mid-bake. |
| **1:10pm** | Mac and cheese out, fully cooked. Keep it covered. |
| **1:16pm** | Oven now at 325°F. Put **rolls in** (raw, full 12 min) **and mac and cheese back in** (already cooked, just reheating covered) **together** — same temp, no conflict, and this keeps the mac and cheese from going lukewarm on the counter. |
| **1:25pm** | Carve the chicken and plate it (it's had ~50 min tented rest at this point — juices are well redistributed). |
| **1:28pm** | Rolls and mac and cheese come out together. |
| **1:29pm** | Uncover mac and cheese, plate rolls, set out Mom's salad. |
| **1:30pm** | Serve — everything hits the table together. |

Notes:
- **The long rest is intentional, not a compromise.** ~50 minutes tented is longer than the usual "20 minutes," but for a whole bird it's within safe/recommended range and actually improves juiciness — just tent loosely (tight wrapping steams the skin) and consider an extra kitchen towel over the foil for insulation.
- **The 325°F double-use at 1:16pm** is the trick that keeps the mac and cheese from sitting around cooling for 18 minutes on the counter — it rides along with the rolls at no extra time cost.
- This leaves Sam 1h45m to eat before the 3:15pm departure, with buffer built into both oven-temperature transitions (5–6 min each), so a slightly slow oven won't blow the schedule.

**Holding the chicken safely (no direct heat, no overcooking):**

1. Let it rest tented loosely in foil for ~15 min on the counter (12:35–12:50) — this is normal carryover rest, not extra cooking.
2. Meanwhile, preheat your cooler: fill it with hot tap water, let it sit a few minutes, then dump it out and dry it. This brings the cooler's internal surfaces up to temp so it acts like a warming box instead of just insulation against room temp.
3. At ~12:50, wrap the chicken tightly in foil (juices sealed in) and set it in the preheated cooler. Pack towels around/on top of it to fill dead air space.
4. Leave it closed until service. This will hold it safely above 140°F for well over an hour without any added heat — no risk of drying out since there's no active cooking happening.

**Revised oven sequence (working back from 1:30pm):**

- **12:40** – Oven to 350°F, macaroni in (30 min bake) → done at **1:10**
- **1:10** – Pull macaroni, tent with foil to hold warm. Drop oven to 325°F (small swing, adjusts fast).
- **1:12** – Rolls in (12 min bake) → done at **1:24**
- **1:24–1:30** – Rolls rest briefly, chicken comes out of the cooler, everything plates together for **1:30 service**.

This gives you a few minutes of buffer and keeps the chicken out of the oven entirely after 165°F, so no dry-out risk.

Here's a conservative sequence, ordered from least to most invasive, avoiding both chemical drain cleaner and disposal strain:

**1. Hot water flush**
Boil a kettle, let it cool slightly (not boiling — full boil can stress PVC joints), and pour it slowly down the affected basin. Repeat 2-3 times over a few minutes. This alone clears many soft clogs (grease/fat from holiday cooking is the likely culprit).

**2. Baking soda + hot water**
Not a "chemical cleaner" in the caustic-drain-opener sense — safe for pipes and the disposal. Pour ~1/2 cup baking soda down the drain, follow with hot (not boiling) water. Let sit 15-20 min, then flush with more hot water.

**3. Manual plunging**
- Since it's a double basin, block the *other* drain opening (wet rag or its own stopper) so plunging force doesn't just push air/water back and forth between basins.
- Add a few inches of water to the clogged basin so the plunger has a seal.
- Do NOT run the disposal while plunging — turn it off at the switch first.
- Plunge with firm, steady strokes for 15-20 seconds, then check drainage.

**4. Check/clear the P-trap by hand**
Put a bucket under the trap, loosen the slip nuts, and remove the trap to check for a clog (usually grease/food debris) lodged there — very common after cooking. Clean it out manually and reseat. No tools beyond a wrench/pliers, no chemicals.

**5. Manual (hand-crank) drum auger, if trap is clear**
If the trap itself is clean, feed a hand-crank auger a few feet into the drain line past the trap. Avoid powered augers — too easy to gouge older pipe or dislodge a joint without knowing what's downstream.

**Stop and contact maintenance if you see any of these:**
- Water starts backing up into the *other* basin, the dishwasher, or any other fixture in the unit (tub, other sink) — signals a shared-line clog beyond what's safe to DIY
- Gurgling from other drains when you run this sink
- Sewage odor
- Any water, dampness, or dripping appears under the cabinet that wasn't there before (given the prior shutoff-seal repair here, worth checking that joint specifically while you're under there)
- No improvement at all after the trap-cleaning step — that suggests the clog is further down the shared line, which is a maintenance/plumber job, not a household one
- Standing water that isn't slowly reducing at all (vs. just draining slowly) — could indicate a fuller blockage than described

Given this is Cherrywood, if it does end up needing maintenance, worth noting for the request that no chemical cleaner was used — keeps the diagnosis clean for them.

Reviewed against the Dec27 standing-lane decision. Owen's draft has five things wrong, not one:

**1. Refresh cadence — wrong value.** Draft says weekly; approved cadence is **monthly**. Owen likely conflated the eligibility refresh cadence with Ines's exposure cap (≤3 exposures/week is a scheduling limit, not how often eligibility itself is recomputed). These are two separate cadences and shouldn't share a value.

**2. Usage ceiling check — missing the recency window.** `usage_ceiling_crossed_at IS NOT NULL` is unbounded — it would pass an account whose ceiling was crossed a year ago. The approved signal requires the crossing to have happened **within the prior 14 days**, carried forward from the Sep30 cohort finding (outcomes concentrated in accounts whose ceiling crossing was recent) into the Dec27 standing-lane spec. Needs a date-bound comparison, not a null check.

**3. Admin-activity check — under-specified in two ways.** `any_admin_active_last_30d = true` is a bare boolean with no qualification:
   - It doesn't exclude service-token/automated actions. The approved signal counts only **human** admin actions (this is the same bug class that wrongly admitted G before the fix).
   - It doesn't confirm the admin is **still active at the time of the check** — needs a join to current admin status, not just "acted within 30 days." An admin who acted 20 days ago but has since been deactivated should not qualify.
   Both the action and the actor's current status need to hold.

**4. Suppression — only covers half the required condition.** Draft suppresses on `active_renewal_work = false` only. The approved rule suppresses on **active CS adoption work OR active renewal work** — adoption-case suppression is missing entirely. As written, an account mid-adoption with CS would still be eligible.

This is a common and usually self-resolving situation with card processing — here's how to handle it.

**What's happening**
Restaurants (especially with tips added after the initial swipe) often generate a temporary authorization hold that doesn't get released until the merchant's final settlement batch clears — sometimes a few days later. Since your posted $86.40 already matches your receipt, the pending $86.40 is very likely that original authorization hold still working its way out of your account, not a genuine second charge.

**What to preserve now**
- The receipt (itemized total, tip, final amount) — you already have this matched to the posted charge.
- A screenshot or export of your account activity showing both entries: their exact posted dates, transaction/reference numbers if visible, and current status (posted vs. pending).
- Note the date you're checking (today) so you can track how many days the pending entry has been outstanding since the Dec 29 visit.

**Whether to wait**
Yes — wait before doing anything. Pending authorizations typically drop off within 2–7 business days, and some restaurant/hospitality holds can take up to 10 days depending on the issuer. Since Dec 29 to today (Jan 4) is only about a week, this is still well within normal range. Don't dispute or contact anyone yet.

**What would justify contacting the merchant or issuer**
Escalate only if one of these happens:
1. The pending $86.40 **converts to a second posted charge** (so you now have two settled $86.40 charges instead of one pending + one posted).
2. The pending entry is **still showing after ~10 business days** without resolving or disappearing.
3. The pending amount **changes** to something inconsistent with your receipt (e.g., a different total appears), suggesting it's not the same authorization.

If any of those occur, that's when you'd call the merchant first (they can usually confirm whether it was a duplicate swipe or an auth error) and involve the card issuer only if the merchant can't resolve it or a genuine duplicate charge posts.

The address mismatch shouldn't cause any tax-filing issues — what matters for accuracy is the name, TIN, and dollar amounts, and those all match the year-end statement. The IRS doesn't care about the mailing address on the form.

Address-only mismatches on a 1099-R are usually low-risk, but here's how to handle it properly:

**What to verify first**
1. **Everything else actually matches** — payer name/TIN, Mom's SSA name, recipient TIN (SSN), account/distribution number, gross distribution, taxable amount, distribution code (Box 7), and any federal/state withholding. These are the fields the IRS and state DOR actually match against the return — confirm each one is correct before treating this as a non-issue.
2. **Whether the address error signals a bigger problem** — an old address can mean the administrator has stale account data generally (e.g., wrong beneficiary flag, outdated bank info for future distributions), not just a typo. Worth asking if anything else on file is outdated.
3. **How she's filing** — if paper-filing, the address on the 1099-R isn't transcribed onto her return (her 1040 uses whatever address she puts there), so it won't cause a mismatch with the IRS. If e-filing, same thing — the form's address field isn't a matched field.

**What NOT to do**
Don't assume you need a corrected/reissued 1099-R (the "CORRECTED" box) just for the address. Administrators typically only reissue for errors in amounts, codes, or taxpayer ID — an address-only correction is usually unnecessary paperwork and can delay things if she's trying to file soon.

**What to request from the administrator**
- Ask them to **update the mailing address on file** for future correspondence and future-year 1099-Rs (separate from this year's form).
- Ask them to **confirm in writing** (email is fine) that the SSN/TIN, distribution amount, and distribution code on the form are correct and tied to her account — this gives her something to point to if a discrepancy ever comes up later.
- Only request a formal corrected 1099-R if they tell you the address error stemmed from an account mix-up (e.g., wrong recipient) rather than a simple stale-mailing-list issue.

Bottom line: she can almost certainly file with the form as-is once you've confirmed the substantive fields match, while separately getting the address fixed on file for next year.

Taking the bus tonight is the right call — no working headlight plus a four-mile road ride at dusk is a real visibility risk, and you don't need to gamble that for a trip with no deadline.

**Tonight:** Walk the bike to the bus, load it on the rack, ride home. Your clip light is fine for the walk to the stop.

**Daylight troubleshooting (battery vs. light vs. mount):**
1. **Swap-test the battery** — put a known-good/freshly charged battery in the light. Powers on and stays on → it was the battery (dead cell or bad contact from reseating). Still flickers/dies → battery isn't the culprit.
2. **Isolate the light body** — with a good battery in, flex the light gently and tap the housing/button area while it's on. Flickers with flexing/tapping → internal connection or switch fault in the light itself.
3. **Check the mount separately** — with the light off the mount, in hand, cycle it on/off a few times and let it run 30+ seconds steady. Stable off-mount but flickers on-mount → mount contacts (corrosion, misalignment, or a cracked mount contact point) are the issue, not the light or battery.
4. **Inspect contacts visually** — battery terminals and mount contacts for corrosion or debris; clean with a dry cloth/eraser if present.

That sequence should tell you cleanly whether to replace the battery, the light, or just clean/fix the mount.

Since the lift is outside the image and the sheet isn't torn, you don't need to commit to a repair today — you can stabilize it dry/near-dry and then let the mat placement decide.

**1. Consolidate the fiber flat (no paste yet)**
Lay a sheet of glassine or silicone release paper over the lifted strip and gently work the fiber back down toward the sheet with a bone folder or fingertip, pushing from the still-attached end toward the loose tip. Do this dry first — a surprising amount of a fiber lift will re-lie flat just from gentle pressure.

**2. If it won't stay flat dry, add minimal moisture**
Touch a small brush barely dampened with clean water only to the lifted fiber (not the surrounding paper), press it down under the release paper, then sandwich it between two pieces of blotter and a flat weight (book, glass) overnight. This relaxes the fiber without introducing any adhesive, so it's fully reversible if you later decide to do more.

**3. Test against the mat before deciding anything permanent**
Once flat and dry, lay your actual mat (or a scrap with the same window size) over the piece and check whether the lift falls entirely under the overlap with margin to spare, not right at the reveal edge. If it's cleanly covered, you're done — no repair needed, just note the orientation so it stays under the window if you re-mat later.

**4. Only if it's visible or too close to the reveal**
That's when the wheat-starch paste and offcut are worth reaching for, as a small localized mend rather than anything affecting the image. Hold off cutting the offcut until step 3 tells you whether you actually need it.

**Framework for comparing the two options**

| Dimension | Guided software ($89) | Enrolled agent ($325) |
|---|---|---|
| Complexity fit | Consumer software is built around exactly this kind of return (a handful of standard 1099s, standard deduction) — it's a well-worn path, not an edge case | Same ground gets covered, just with a person doing the data entry and judgment calls |
| Error risk | Interview-driven, reduces omission risk if Mom answers prompts accurately; most providers carry an accuracy guarantee | Professional review adds a second layer of judgment, especially useful if any answer is ambiguous |
| Audit support | Usually limited to "we'll help you understand the notice," not representation, unless a paid add-on | An EA can represent her directly before the IRS if anything is ever questioned |
| Time/effort | Requires Mom to sit through the interview and gather documents herself | Largely hands-off once documents are delivered |
| Future value | One-and-done, no ongoing relationship | If her situation is likely to get more complex later, having an EA already familiar with her return has compounding value |
| Price delta | — | $236 more — worth pricing out what that specifically buys |

**Questions worth having Mom answer before choosing**

1. Is the health-insurance coverage through an ACA marketplace plan (which would mean a Form 1095-A and premium-tax-credit reconciliation) or employer/Medicare coverage (1095-B/C, generally simpler)? This is the one item in her document list that could meaningfully change the complexity picture.
2. Does she want to do the data entry herself, or would she strongly prefer to hand everything off and not touch it?
3. Does she specifically want audit representation as part of the service, or just accuracy checking?
4. What exactly is included in the EA's $325 quote — e-filing, a state return if needed, audit support, availability for questions later in the year? Software pricing often excludes state filing as an add-on too, so both quotes should be compared on an apples-to-apples basis.
5. Does she expect her tax situation to stay this simple next year, or might it get more complex (which would make an ongoing EA relationship more valuable than a one-time software purchase)?
6. Is a state return required, and does that change the cost comparison for either option?

I haven't assessed whether she'd qualify for any deduction or credit, and haven't touched the actual return — this is just the decision scaffolding for her to work through.

Based on the current facts (1.5" fiber lift, stable and flat after a week under a blotter, pigment/image unaffected, sheet not torn, mat overlapping the damage by ~1/4"), you can leave it unrepaired and mat over it as planned — this matches the conservative "stabilize and monitor" approach you've defaulted to on the last few tape-lift occurrences ([[user_watercolor_tape_lift_pattern]]) rather than applying the wheat-starch paste preemptively.

Signs that would justify professional repair (paper conservator) instead of just leaving it under the mat:

- **Progression** — the lift grows or starts spreading again after a period of being flat, rather than staying static.
- **Fiber loss, not just displacement** — bits of fiber flake off or crumble rather than lying raised but intact.
- **A true tear or split** develops (a structural break through the sheet) rather than a surface-fiber lift.
- **The margin closes** — if the lift's footprint grows enough to erase the ~1/4" buffer under the mat, so it would sit right at or past the mat window edge.
- **Cockling/buckling** at that edge, suggesting the damage runs deeper than surface fibers.
- **Contact risk at assembly** — if you're float-mounting or the glazing will sit close enough to touch the paper (no mat spacer), the raised fiber could abrade against glass over time; that's a reason to consolidate first even if otherwise stable.

Practical check: re-inspect right before you seal the frame (once you place the actual mat, not just the planned one) to confirm it still lies flat and the coverage margin holds. If none of the above shows up, no paste, no conservator — just proceed with matting.

But two things need clarifying before calling these "operationally useful" rather than just plausible-looking round numbers:

2. **Planned downtime.** A maintenance window over 2 hours will fire warning/critical with no actionable signal behind it. Needs either a suppression window or a "known-maintenance" label rather than tuning the threshold around it.

- Lag = consumer as-of minus source as-of; both timestamps always shown alongside the state (OK/warning/critical).
- Warning >2hr, critical >4hr, computed off refresh-attempt cadence, not data-change cadence (pending Daniela's confirmation of which she's using).
- Explicitly labeled as an *operational alert trigger*, not the governed per-field freshness bound from the still-open state-contract checklist — these thresholds can move without a new approval since they're not that decision.

**Prior-year AGI** is used only for identity verification with the IRS e-file system (the "Self-Select PIN" process). **The IRA-vs-pension prompt**, by contrast, is driven by fields on the 1099-R itself:

- **Box 2a (Taxable amount)** vs **Box 1 (Gross distribution)** — if these differ, or if **Box 2b "Taxable amount not determined"** is checked, the taxable portion isn't fully settled by the form itself.

- The distribution code is anything other than a plain "7" (e.g., 1, 2, 4, G, or a combination) — these change tax treatment materially.

That reject code (IND-031-04) means the IRS's e-file system didn't match the AGI on file — it's not about what's printed on last year's return, but what the IRS actually has recorded for it. A few common causes and fixes, in order of likelihood:

1. **Last year's return was processed late** (filed after ~mid-November, filed on paper, or amended) — the IRS's verification database often isn't updated in time for e-file matching the following year. Fix: **re-enter AGI as `0`** instead of the actual number. This is the standard workaround the IRS itself recommends in this situation, and it resolves the majority of IND-031-04 rejects.
2. **Return was amended** — if last year's return was corrected after original filing, the IRS may be matching against the *original* filed AGI, not the amended one (or vice versa).
3. **Filing status changed** — e.g., if she filed jointly last year and separately this year (or vice versa), some software mis-splits the AGI between spouses.

If entering `0` doesn't clear it, the reliable way to get the exact number the IRS has on file is her **IRS Online Account** or a **Tax Return Transcript** (irs.gov/individuals/get-transcript) — that shows the AGI as the IRS's system has it, which can differ from her copy if anything was adjusted after filing.

Suggest she try `0` first since that's the fastest fix and most likely to be the cause, then resubmit.

Here's a stepwise approach for the IND-031-04 rejection (prior-year AGI mismatch):

1. **Confirm which AGI was actually entered.** IRS wants the AGI from her **originally filed** prior-year return — not a later amended return, and not the "corrected" AGI if the IRS adjusted it after filing. If she amended last year's return, the original (pre-amendment) AGI is still what's required.

2. **Check filing-status nuances.** If her filing status changed year-over-year (e.g., joint last year, single/HOH this year, or vice versa), each person uses their own individual prior-year AGI, not the joint figure.

3. **Verify whether last year's return had actually finished processing before she filed this year.** If last year's return was filed late (e.g., an extension, or filed close to the following year's filing season) and hadn't fully posted to the IRS master file yet, the IRS system won't have an AGI to match against — even a correct entry will bounce.

4. **Pull an IRS transcript to get the authoritative number**, rather than re-guessing from her own copy. Use the "Get Transcript Online" tool at IRS.gov (or Get Transcript by Mail if she can't verify identity online) and request the **Tax Return Transcript** for the prior year — it shows the AGI exactly as the IRS has it on record. Re-enter that exact figure.

5. **If the transcript confirms the return wasn't processed in time** (no transcript available yet, or it shows as not-yet-posted), enter **$0** for prior-year AGI instead. This is the standard IRS workaround specifically for cases where the prior return wasn't in the system yet — don't use $0 as a first guess, only after confirming via transcript that processing is the actual cause.

6. **If it still rejects after trying the transcript AGI and then $0**, stop iterating on AGI entries. At that point, either paper-file this year's return, or check whether she has an IRS Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) on file — an IP PIN can be used for identity verification instead of the AGI match.

Given memory notes she can now see the prior-year AGI in the software — worth double-checking that displayed figure against an actual transcript pull rather than assuming the software's number is correct, since a software display error (or original-vs-amended confusion) is a common silent cause of this exact reject code.

Here's a practical assessment based on what you've described.

**Should you drive it?**
An 8 psi overnight drop (35→27, ~23% loss) with a visible screw near the center tread is a classic slow-leak pattern from a tread puncture — generally repairable, and the tire isn't failing catastrophically. Since you don't hear hissing or see sidewall damage, it's not an emergency-stop situation, but 27 psi is under-inflated enough that driving on it stresses the sidewalls and can cause heat buildup or bead damage, especially at higher speeds or over distance.

- **If the tire shop is close (a few miles) and you can air it up first:** reasonable to drive, but only after reinflating to the full 35 psi with a portable inflator, and only if it holds air long enough to get there (check pressure again right before leaving — if it's already back down near 27 or lower, don't go).
- **If the shop is farther, or pressure keeps dropping while you're filling it:** don't drive on it. Call the shop for mobile tire service, use roadside assistance/tow, or swap to the spare if you're comfortable doing that.
- Keep speed low (under ~45 mph) and avoid highways for this trip regardless.

**Should you leave the screw in place?**
Yes — leave it in. The screw may be partially plugging the hole, and pulling it could turn a slow leak into a fast one, potentially stranding you or causing loss of control while driving. Removal and proper repair (patch/plug from the inside, or replacement if it's a sidewall/shoulder puncture) should be done by the shop, not before.

**Adding air solely for a short trip — is it reasonable?**
Yes, this is a normal and safe practice *if*:
- The puncture is truly center-tread (not sidewall) — sounds consistent with what you're describing.
- You inflate to the full recommended 35 psi, not just "enough."
- The trip is short and direct, at reduced speed.
- You're not seeing rapid audible hissing, visible sidewall bulge, or the tire going flat again in the few minutes it takes to check before departure.

If any of those conditions aren't met, treat it as "do not drive" and get the car to the tire instead of the tire to the shop (mobile service or tow).

Based on the concrete signs you're describing, this is a non-event — safe to close out:

- **24°F freezer temp**: well below the 40°F threshold where refreeze/food-safety risk starts to matter.
- **Chicken and frozen vegetables**: still hard with visible ice crystals — never left the safe zone, no action needed.
- **Bread**: still frozen — fine.
- **Ice cream**: soft at the edges but still cold and partly frozen — this is a quality issue (texture may go a bit grainy from the partial thaw), not a safety one, since it never got into the danger zone.
- No leaking or raw-food cross-contact, so no contamination path either.

Nothing here needs discarding, retesting, or ongoing temperature monitoring — just close the freezer door and go about things normally.

**Assessment approach:** Don't judge by look, smell, or taste — for a 3‑hour ajar interval, the deciding factor is whether each item is still ≤40°F (4°C) at its core and still has ice crystals. Check with a food thermometer inserted into the center of a representative package in each category; a working freezer thermometer (not the dial) is the only way to confirm this reliably.

**Keep (generally safe, refreeze with likely quality loss):**
- Fruits — low risk regardless of thaw state; refreeze or use.
- Most vegetables — safe if still cold/ice crystals present; texture may soften.
- Bread, baked goods, most grains/flour products.
- Butter/margarine.

**Conditional — check temp/ice crystals before deciding:**
- Raw meat, poultry, fish — refreeze or cook immediately only if still ≤40°F with ice crystals intact. If it's climbed above 40°F and you can't confirm it was for under 2 cumulative hours, discard.
- Hard cheeses, shredded cheese.

**Discard if there's any doubt (high-risk, low margin for error):**
- Cooked leftovers, casseroles, soups, stews.
- Eggs/egg products, cream-based items.
- Ice cream and other frozen dairy desserts (dairy + repeated thaw/refreeze is a bad combination even if it looks fine).
- Anything that has fully lost its ice crystals and is soft/limp in a high-risk category.

Given only a 3‑hour ajar window, most items in a reasonably full freezer likely never crossed 40°F — but confirm per-item rather than assuming, since packages near the door thaw faster than ones buried in the back.

**Restoring the freezer:**
1. Close the door and check the gasket/seal isn't obstructed by a package or ice buildup — that's the most common reason a door goes ajar unnoticed.
2. Temporarily set it to the coldest setting to speed recovery back to 0°F (-18°C), then return to the normal setting once stable.
3. Avoid opening it again for several hours while it recovers.

**Monitoring after:**
- Place an appliance thermometer at the center of the freezer (not relying on the built-in dial) and check it over the next 4–6 hours until it reads 0°F/-18°C consistently.
- Re-check the borderline items you kept once the freezer has re-stabilized to make sure they're solidly refrozen, not just surface-frozen.
- Do not use smell or taste at any point to re-verify safety — the bacteria of concern here don't reliably change either.
